name: Calpurnius Siculus
bio: Titus Calpurnius Siculus was a Latin pastoral poet of the first century AD. Nothing is known of his life beyond what his seven Eclogues suggest: they are written in the manner of Virgil's Eclogues and look to a young emperor, generally taken to be Nero, whose accession (AD 54) is greeted in the first poem as the start of a new golden age. His second name, Siculus, has been read as marking a Sicilian origin, but it may be only a literary echo of the Sicilian muse of Theocritus and Virgil.

The Eclogues set shepherds singing in turn: a prophecy of peace carved by Faunus on a beech tree, a singing match judged by Thyrsis, a lovers' quarrel mended by a letter cut into bark, and a long praise of the emperor. The fifth poem is a shepherd's lesson in husbandry, and the seventh describes the wooden amphitheatre and its shows as seen by a countryman come up to Rome. The poems survived with those of the later poet Nemesianus, and older editions print his four eclogues after these as the eighth to eleventh; here Calpurnius stands alone.
